entities.name: Blue Mosque
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Blue Mosque (Sultan Ahmed Mosque, Sultanahmet Camii) is the most famous mosque in Istanbul, built between 1609 and 1616 CE by Ottoman Sultan Ahmed I. Distinguished by its six minarets — unusual and once controversial, as six minarets had previously been the exclusive prerogative of the Masjid al-Haram in Mecca — the mosque's interior features 20,000 hand-painted İznik tiles in shades of blue and turquoise that give it its popular name.

Sultan Ahmed I commissioned the mosque at age 19 to demonstrate Ottoman piety and power, building it directly across from the Byzantine Hagia Sophia. The architect Sedefkâr Mehmed Ağa created a mosque with five main domes, eight secondary domes, and six minarets that dominates Istanbul's skyline. The 20,000 İznik tiles, created in more than 50 different tulip designs, cover the interior walls in one of the greatest displays of Ottoman decorative ceramics.

The mosque remains an active place of worship and closes to tourists during the five daily prayer times. Its construction is considered the last great mosque of the classical Ottoman period before a long architectural decline. The mosque sits at the center of Sultanahmet Square in Istanbul's historic center, facing Hagia Sophia across an open plaza — a deliberately staged dialogue between Byzantine and Ottoman architectural achievement. Both buildings were designated UNESCO World Heritage sites as part of the Historic Areas of Istanbul (1985).

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Blue Mosque's six minarets and 20,000 İznik tiles represent the apex of Ottoman decorative achievement, while its deliberate positioning facing Hagia Sophia embodies Ottoman civilization's self-conscious dialogue with Byzantine heritage.
